accepted.question_text: Classify all recurrent one-sided sequences x in A^N and two-sided sequences x in A^Z whose maximal pattern complexity satisfies p*(n)=2n for every n >= 1. Equivalently, determine exactly which sequences are pattern Sturmian in the sense of Kamae and Zamboni.

evidence.quote: The sequence x is pattern Sturmian if p∗ (n) = 2n for all n ≥ 1. Note that a Sturmian sequence is necessarily pattern Sturmian. The converse inclusion, however, does not hold. Problem 2.1.1. Determine all single sided (resp. double sided) sequences that are pattern Sturmian.

accepted.question_text: Let λ be a complex number and let x be a {0,1}-valued pattern Sturmian sequence. For the discrete Schrödinger operator H on l^2(Z) defined by [Hψ](m)=ψ(m+1)+ψ(m-1)+λ x_m ψ(m), must the spectrum σ(H) be a Cantor set of Lebesgue measure zero, and must all spectral measures be singular continuous?

evidence.quote: Theorem 2.1.1. Let λ ∈ C and let x ∈ {0, 1}^Z be a Sturmian sequence. Denote by H the Schrödinger operator defined in the space l2 (Z) as follows : given ψ ∈ l2 (Z) and m ∈ Z, let [Hψ] (m) := ψ(m + 1) + ψ(m − 1) + λ · xm · ψ(m). Then, the spectrum σ(H) of the operator H is a zero Lebesgue measure Cantor set. Furthermore, all spectral measures are singular continuous.
Conjecture 2.1.1. Theorem 2.1.1 holds if x is a pattern Sturmian sequence.

accepted.question_text: For the graph (V,E) of the Penrose tiling, consider the operator H on l^2(V) defined by [Hψ](v)=sum_{w:(v,w) in E}(ψ(w)-ψ(v)). Determine the spectrum σ(H) of this operator.

evidence.quote: The spectrum of Schrödinger operators associated with quasicrystal models in higher dimensions is not well understood. Consider for example the Penrose tiling and the corresponding graph (V, E), where V is the vertex set and E the set of edges. Define the operator H in the space l2 (V ) as follows : for any ψ ∈ l2 (V ) and any v ∈ V , let [Hψ](v) := sum_{w : (v,w)∈E} (ψ(w) − ψ(v)). Problem 2.1.2. Determine the spectrum σ(H) of the operator defined above.

accepted.question_text: Let γ=(sqrt(5)-1)/2. For λ1, λ2 in C, define one-dimensional potentials s_j^{λ_j}(k)=λ_j χ_[1-γ,1)({kγ}) for j in {1,2}, and define V(m,n)=s_1^{λ_1}(m)+s_2^{λ_2}(n). Let H be the Schrödinger operator on l^2(Z^2) given by [Hψ](m,n)=ψ(m+1,n)+ψ(m-1,n)+ψ(m,n+1)+ψ(m,n-1)+V(m,n)ψ(m,n). Do there exist values of λ1 and λ2 for which the spectrum σ(H) is a Cantorval, meaning the spectrum is the closure of its interior and has no isolated connected component?

evidence.quote: Another example of a two dimensional problem arises when considering a two dimensional potential V that can be written as a sum of two one dimensional potentials s_{λ1}^1 and s_{λ2}^2. Here, λ1 , λ2 ∈ C and, for j ∈ {1, 2} and k ∈ Z, s_j^{λ_j} (k) := λj · χ[1−γ,1) ({kγ}) with γ = (sqrt(5)-1)/2. Thus, for any m, n ∈ Z, V (m, n) := s_1^{λ_1} (m) + s_2^{λ_2} (n). The corresponding Schrödinger operator H in the space l2 (Z2 ) is defined as follows : for ψ ∈ l2 (Z) and (m, n) ∈ Z2 , [Hψ](m, n) := ψ(m + 1, n) + ψ(m − 1, n) + ψ(m, n + 1) + ψ(m, n − 1) + V (m, n) · ψ(m, n).
Conjecture 2.1.2. There exist values of λ1 and λ2 such that the spectrum σ(H) of H is a Cantorval; that is, the spectrum is the closure of its interior and no connected component is isolated.

accepted.question_text: Let λ>1 be a Pisot number and let a one-dimensional self-similar inflation tiling have scaling factor λ and abelianisation matrix M. If the characteristic polynomial of M is irreducible, equivalently if the algebraic degree of λ equals the dimension of M or the number of tile types, must the tiling dynamical system have pure point spectrum?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.2.1 (Pisot Substitution Conjecture). A one–dimensional self–similar inflation tiling with Pisot scaling factor λ has pure point spectrum if its abelianisation matrix (i.e. its substitution matrix) M has an irreducible characteristic polynomial; that is, if the algebraic degree of λ equals the dimension of M (or the number of tile types).

accepted.question_text: For a one-dimensional unimodular Pisot inflation tiling with scaling factor λ, if the first rational Čech cohomology group has rank equal to the algebraic degree of λ, must the tiling have pure point spectrum?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.2.2 (Homological Pisot Conjecture). A one–dimensional, unimodular Pisot inflation tiling has pure point spectrum if its first rational Čech cohomology group has rank equal to the algebraic degree of λ.

accepted.question_text: For a one-dimensional Pisot inflation tiling with scaling factor λ, must the coincidence rank divide the algebraic norm of λ? Here the coincidence rank is the almost-everywhere multiplicity of the factor map from the tiling dynamical system to its maximal equicontinuous factor.

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.2.3 (Coincidence Rank Conjecture). The coincidence rank of a one–dimensional Pisot inflation tiling must divide the algebraic norm of λ.
The coincidence rank is the multiplicity (almost everywhere) of the factor map to the maximal equicontinuous factor of the tiling dynamical system. It must be one for pure point spectrum.

accepted.question_text: For a Pinwheel tiling of the plane, place a point mass at the natural reference point of each tile and consider the resulting Dirac comb. Its diffraction measure is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation and is known to have circular symmetry. Determine where the sharp rings occur in this diffraction measure and compute their intensities.

evidence.quote: A Pinwheel Tiling is then defined as a tiling of the plane whose tiles are isometric copies of T, in which a tile may intersect another tile only either on a whole side or on half the length 2 side, and such that the following property holds : the tiles of any Pinwheel Tiling can be grouped in sets of five into homothetic tiles, so that these homothetic tiles form (up to rescaling) a new Pinwheel Tiling.

Choose a reference point (a natural choice is the point at coordinates (1/2, 1/2) with respect to the vertex point at the right–angled corner of the triangular tile) and consider a uniform Dirac comb obtained by placing a point measure at each reference point. The diffraction measure is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation and is a well–defined positive measure.

There are arguments that support the existence of such ‘sharp rings’ in the diffraction measure of the pinwheel tiling ... However, none of these properties has yet been proved. Problem 2.3.1. Determine the position of sharp rings in the diffraction measure of a Pinwheel Tiling and their intensity.

accepted.question_text: For the diffraction measure of the Dirac comb associated with a Pinwheel tiling, does there exist an absolutely continuous component in addition to the known trivial pure point mass at the origin and the continuous part already established?

evidence.quote: It is known that this measure has circular symmetry and, as a consequence, the only pure point part of it is the trivial point measure at the origin, which is related to the density. Apart from this point measure, the diffraction measure is continuous.

Numerical investigations also indicate the presence of additional components which might be absolutely continuous. However, none of these properties has yet been proved. Problem 2.3.2. Does the diffraction measure of the Pinwheel Tiling contain an absolutely continuous component?

accepted.question_text: Let Ω be the tiling space of an aperiodic repetitive tiling of dimension d, and let p(n) count patches of radius n up to translation. If p(n)=O(n^d), must the rational Čech cohomology of Ω be finitely generated, equivalently must rk(H^*(Ω,Q)) be finite?

evidence.quote: In higher dimensions, the complexity function of a tiling counts in an analogous way the number of patches of radius n (up to translation).
Problem 2.5.1. With the same notation, is it the case that for an aperiodic, repetitive tiling of dimension d, if p(n) = O(nd), then rk(H ∗ (Ω, Q)) < ∞?

accepted.question_text: Let D be a Delone set in R^2 that is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to Z^2. Does there exist a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism L:R^2→R^2 such that L(D)=Z^2?

evidence.quote: Two point sets in Rd are bi-Lipschitz equivalent (abbreviated BL) if there is a bi-Lipschitz bijection between them.
Problem 2.6.1. Let D ⊂ R2 be a Delone set BL to Z2. Does there exist a bi–Lipschitz map L : R2 → R2 such that L(D) = Z2 ?

accepted.question_text: Classify the geometric properties P of tilings that are inherited by every tiling in the same equivalence class under mutual local derivability, topological conjugacy, or homeomorphism. The motivating examples in the paper are properties such as bounded-displacement equivalence to a lattice, bi-Lipschitz equivalence to a lattice, and linear repetitivity.
accepted.context_brief: Geometric properties invariant under tiling equivalence

evidence.quote: Two point sets in Rd are bounded displacement equivalent (abbreviated BD) if there is a bijection between them which moves every point by at most some finite amount. Two point sets in Rd are bi-Lipschitz equivalent (abbreviated BL) if there is a bi-Lipschitz bijection between them.

A pattern Y ⊆ Rd is linearly repetitive (abbreviated LR) if there exists a constant C > 0 such that, for every r ≥ 1, every patch of size r which occurs anywhere in Y, occurs in every ball of radius Cr in Rd. The abbreviation MLD stands for mutually locally derivable.
Problem 2.7.1. Classify tilings with such a property that any other tiling MLD (or topologically conjugate, or homeomorphic) to it also has that property.

accepted.question_text: Develop and study new geometric properties of tilings, analogous to bounded-displacement equivalence, bi-Lipschitz equivalence, or similar geometric notions, that are invariant under mutual local derivability, topological conjugacy, or homeomorphism.

evidence.quote: Problem 2.7.2. Develop and study new geometric properties, analogous but not identical to BD, BL, etc., that are invariant under MLD, topological conjugacy, or homeomorphism.

accepted.question_text: Find local matching rules for quasicrystal tilings in dimension 2 or 3 such that both of the following hold. First, for every tile type t and every finite region R made of tiles, the discrepancy D_t(R)=|N_t(R)-d(t)vol(R)| is bounded by c_t |∂R| for some constant c_t depending only on t, where N_t(R) counts tiles of type t in R and d(t) is the density of t. Second, the same perimeter-order discrepancy bound holds for every pattern or patch that satisfies the matching rules.
accepted.context_brief: Matching rules with perimeter discrepancy bounds

evidence.quote: (A) Given a tile t and a region R of the tiling space made of a finite union of tiles, define the discrepancy Dt (R) of the tile t in R as Dt (R) := |Nt (R) − d(t) · vol(R)|. Here, Nt (R) stands for the cardinality of the number of tiles t in the region R and d(t) for the density of the tile t. The first condition imposed on the tiling is that of 'low fluctuation'; that is, that there exists a constant ct depending only on the tile t such that Dt (R) ≤ ct · |∂R|.

(B) The second condition is that property (A) should also hold for any pattern or patch satisfying the given matching rule. Problem 2.7.3. Find a set of matching rules in dimension 2 and/or 3 that meet both condition (A) and condition (B).

accepted.question_text: Find local matching rules in dimension 2 for which the discrepancy of every tile type t in every finite tiled region R satisfies D_t(R)=|N_t(R)-d(t)vol(R)| <= c_t |∂R| for some constant c_t depending only on t.

evidence.quote: The following statement can be seen as a first step to the solution of Problem 2.7.3 : Problem 2.7.4. Find a set of matching rules in dimension 2 satisfying condition (A) only.
The first condition imposed on the tiling is that of 'low fluctuation'; that is, that there exists a constant ct depending only on the tile t such that Dt (R) ≤ ct · |∂R|.

accepted.question_text: Let Cl(R^d) be the compact metric space of closed subsets of R^d with the Chabauty-Fell topology. Determine all Borel probability measures on Cl(R^d) that are invariant under the natural action of SL_d(R), and likewise determine all such measures invariant under the natural action of ASL_d(R).

evidence.quote: Let d ≥ 1 be an integer. Denote by Cl(Rd ) the set of all closed subsets of Rd with respect to the Chabauty–Fell topology [1]. Thus, Cl(Rd ) is a compact metric space and any group acting on Rd acts on it by transporting closed sets. Let SLd (R) denote the group of matrices in dimension d with determinant one, viz. the group of all volume and orientation preserving linear transformations in Rd . Let ASLd (R) denote the affine group in Rd , viz. the group of all orientation and volume preserving affine maps in Rd .
Problem 2.8.1 (J. Marklof). Determine all SLd(R)–invariant Borel probability measures on Cl(Rd) and similarly for the ASLd(R) action.

accepted.question_text: Let E be a totally irrational d-dimensional subspace of R^k, and let Y be a cut-and-project set obtained from E using a bounded window W with non-empty interior such that the (k-d)-dimensional Lebesgue measure of the boundary ∂W is zero. Must Y always be bi-Lipschitz equivalent to a lattice in E?

evidence.quote: Two point sets in Rd are bi-Lipschitz equivalent (abbreviated BL) if there is a bi-Lipschitz bijection between them.

Problem 2.8.2. Let E ⊂ Rk be a totally irrational subspace of dimension d ≥ 1, and let Y be a cut–and–project set obtained from E using a bounded window W with non–empty interior and with the property that the (k − d)–dimensional Lebesgue measure of ∂W is zero. Is such a set Y always BL to a lattice in E?

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 2.4.1. Is there a choice of α and β as above such that sup_{Ω∈S} #ξ_(α,β)(Ω) = +∞, where S denotes the collection of all aligned squares?

evidence.quote: Let α, β ∈ R be such that 1, α and β are Q–linearly independent. Let Y(α, β) be a canonical cut–and–project set formed using the subspace E(α, β) := {(x, y, αx + βy) : x, y ∈ R} ⊂ R3. Given a shape Ω ⊂ E(α, β), let ξ_(α,β)(Ω) denote the set of different frequencies of patches of shape Ω in Y(α, β) which occur in E(α, β).

Problem 2.4.1. Is there a choice of α and β as above such that sup #ξ_(α,β)(Ω) = +∞, where S denotes the collection of all aligned squares? The precise definition of an aligned square (resp. of an aligned rectangle) can be found in [4].

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 2.4.2. Is there a choice of α and β as above such that sup_{Ω∈R} #ξ_(α,β)(Ω) = +∞, where R denotes the collection of aligned rectangles?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.4.2. Is there a choice of α and β as above such that sup #ξ_(α,β)(Ω) = +∞, where R denotes the collection of aligned rectangles?
The precise definition of an aligned square (resp. of an aligned rectangle) can be found in [4].

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 2.4.3. Given (α, β) ∈ R^2 such that 1, α and β are Q-linearly independent, does lim inf_{n→∞} n ||nα|| ||nβ|| = 0 imply Problem 2.4.2's condition sup_{Ω∈R} #ξ_(α,β)(Ω) = +∞?

evidence.quote: There is currently no known example of a pair (α, β) for which (2) holds. Using the arguments in [4] and [5], it can be shown that any such pair satisfies the equation lim inf n ||nα|| ||nβ|| = 0. Whether the converse holds is an open problem : Problem 2.4.3. Given (α, β) ∈ R2 such that 1, α and β are Q–linearly independent, does (3) imply (2)?
